issues.description: The manuscript gives inconsistent definitions of the temporal window for suicide attempt episodes. One section defines attempt episodes as the one-week period prior to the attempt, while elsewhere the analyses and hypotheses are framed around two weeks preceding the attempt. This inconsistency makes it unclear what data were actually analyzed and undermines reproducibility and interpretation of all time-based findings.
issues.quote: During the interview, participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place. Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a “suicide attempt episode”; ... The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made in a conservative effort to capture the critical period...

issues.description: The Discussion claims that mean-difference analyses showed greater anxiety and sadness during high-risk periods, but the Results explicitly state that only sadness showed a significant effect of episode type and that anxiety was not significant. This discrepancy overstates findings and may mislead readers about what was supported.
issues.quote: Results: "No significant effects by episode type emerged for more general emotional content ... or other specific emotions/constructs (i.e., anxiety, anger, death)." Discussion: "results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness."

issues.description: Throughout the Results and tables, the likelihood-ratio chi-square statistic is reported incorrectly as "2(3)=..." instead of the standard χ²(3)=... . This is not merely stylistic because it obscures what test was conducted and suggests possible reporting carelessness in inferential results.
issues.quote: "Regarding sentiment, there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003."

issues.description: The text reports p=.003 for the episode-type effect on sadness, but Table 2 reports p=.033 for the same χ²=8.74 with df=3. For χ²=8.74, p≈.033 is plausible, not .003. This discrepancy changes the apparent strength of evidence and indicates a likely statistical reporting error.
issues.quote: Results text: "there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003." Table 2: "Sadness (sad) | 2=8.74 | 3 | 3 | .033"

issues.description: The manuscript states that desire to die significantly decreased slightly from pre to post, but the reported means increase from 0.82 to 1.03. Either the means are reversed, the sign of the t-test is wrong, or the interpretation is incorrect. This is a basic inconsistency in statistical interpretation.
issues.quote: "desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033."

issues.description: One pairwise comparison reports p=.0111 while all other p-values are given to three decimals. This may be typographical, but it raises concern about inconsistent reporting standards and potential transcription errors in inferential output.
issues.quote: "including ideation (z=2.00, p=.046), depressed (z=2.49, p=.013), and positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes"

issues.description: The manuscript describes β as "standardized values" and as effect sizes for mixed models, but the GLMM coefficients are in log-odds units and are not standardized by default in lme4. Presenting them as standardized effect sizes is incorrect and can mislead readers about comparability across outcomes.
issues.quote: "Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes."

issues.description: The power analysis is based on chi-square tests and Cramer's V for mixed-effects models, with unclear derivation of a "design effect" and contradictory sample assumptions. This is not an appropriate or transparent power analysis for the specified multilevel GLMM/LMM analyses, so claims about adequate power are not well supported.
issues.quote: "We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models comparing suicide attempts to other types of episodes..."

issues.description: The analyses are conducted at the individual-message level on 189,478 texts, which can create an impression of a very large sample despite only 27 participants contributing usable SMS episodes. Without clearly modeling the dependence structure induced by many messages from the same conversations/days/contacts, standard errors may be anti-conservative and effective sample size overstated.
issues.quote: "This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode..."

issues.description: The core predictor (episode type and dates) is based on retrospective self-identification of past suicidal and mood episodes, including exact dates. This design is highly vulnerable to recall bias and post hoc reconstruction, especially for emotionally salient events and for assigning day-by-day windows that drive slope analyses.
issues.quote: "participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes, including dates of past suicide attempts ... and two-week episodes of suicide ideation, depressive mood, and positive mood."

issues.description: The study combines actual, interrupted, and aborted attempts under a single "suicide attempt episode" category, and even includes episodes where no physical attempt occurred but participants subjectively felt intent was higher than ideation. This substantially broadens and blurs the outcome construct, making the 'attempt' category heterogeneous and potentially not comparable to standard definitions of suicide attempt.
issues.quote: "reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions."

issues.description: By including aborted/interrupted events and even subjectively self-endorsed attempts without enactment, the operationalization of "suicide attempt" does not align with the standard construct of an actual self-injurious act with at least some intent to die. This threatens construct validity of all comparisons purportedly distinguishing attempt from ideation.
issues.quote: "suicide attempts (defined as actual, interrupted, and aborted attempts)"

issues.subcategory: positive episode mislabeled as typical mood
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently describes the low-risk comparator as "positive mood" in some sections and as "typical mood" in methods. These are conceptually distinct states. If the comparison condition varies between positive and neutral/typical mood, interpretation of language differences is compromised.
issues.quote: "two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt)." ... elsewhere: "periods of positive mood"

issues.description: The target low-risk episode is referred to across the manuscript as "positive mood," "typical mood," and "positive episodes." These are not equivalent categories. This inconsistency makes it unclear what state participants were asked to recall and what data entered the analyses.
issues.quote: "episodes included ... 4) two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt)." ... "depressed mood, and positive mood."

issues.description: The study treats singular first-person pronoun use as an indicator of rumination/self-focus. This is a tenuous operationalization because pronoun use is influenced by grammar, context, message recipient, and conversational function, and does not directly measure maladaptive self-focused attention or rumination. Overinterpreting this proxy may lead to invalid construct inferences.
issues.quote: "we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts"

issues.subcategory: social engagement measured by sent/received ratios
issues.description: The interpersonal theory constructs of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness are operationalized as aggregate ratios of outgoing to incoming texts. These message counts are weak proxies for these psychological constructs and may reflect phone habits, social network size, logistics, or texting norms rather than belongingness or burdensomeness.
issues.quote: "we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages."

issues.description: LIWC single-word categories are used to infer sentiment and emotional state, but the paper itself later acknowledges inability to capture negation and context. Given this limitation, drawing psychological conclusions about acute suicide risk from isolated word categories is construct-weak and should be more cautiously framed from the outset.
issues.quote: "One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., “not happy” would count as “positive emotion” because negation is not accounted for)"

issues.subcategory: causal language from observational retrospective data
issues.description: The paper repeatedly frames identified text features as markers that could determine when someone is at imminent risk, and uses predictive language despite a retrospective, nonexperimental design with self-labeled episodes. The analyses show associations, not validated real-time prediction or causal indicators of imminent risk.
issues.quote: "Objective tools to assess suicide risk are needed to determine when someone is at imminent risk." ... "Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk."

issues.subcategory: claim of prospective design despite retrospective reconstruction
issues.description: The manuscript describes the study as utilizing a "prospective research design" because it reconstructs timelines retrospectively. This is conceptually incorrect. The design is retrospective observational, and calling it prospective overstates causal/predictive strength.
issues.quote: "By reconstructing the timeline of recent suicidal behaviors through a retrospective clinical interview, we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt"

issues.description: The paper repeatedly states that text features predicted suicide attempt or could identify imminent risk in real time, but no prospective prediction, classifier validation, or out-of-sample evaluation is reported in this manuscript. Inferential mixed models on retrospectively defined episodes do not establish predictive utility.
issues.quote: "we aimed to improve our ability to assess suicide risk dynamically in real time." ... "understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt"

issues.subcategory: post hoc selection of time window
issues.description: Although the two-week window is described as chosen a priori, the manuscript also states that the optimal window was assessed empirically by visual inspection of loess-smoothed plots over 30 days. This data-driven tuning of the analysis window introduces researcher degrees of freedom and risks capitalizing on chance, especially in a small pilot study.
issues.quote: "The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made... The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced."

issues.description: The authors acknowledge running a fairly large number of tests and intentionally do not correct for multiple comparisons. In a small exploratory pilot with many outcomes and pairwise contrasts, this materially inflates false-positive risk, particularly for marginal p-values near .05 that anchor the main conclusions.
issues.quote: "Given this is a pilot study ... we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)"

issues.description: The manuscript says features were selected a priori and materials are on OSF, but it does not specify whether hypotheses, outcomes, time windows, model structures, exclusion rules, or supplemental robustness analyses were preregistered before data inspection. This leaves substantial analytic flexibility unaccounted for.
issues.quote: "we analyzed and compared text messages during episodes within person based on a number of features selected a priori"

issues.subcategory: changing random-effects structure after convergence failure
issues.description: For the time-interaction models, the planned maximal random-effects structure did not converge and all random slopes were removed. Dropping random slopes can materially affect Type I error and estimates. The manuscript does not report attempts at principled simplification, alternative optimizers, or sensitivity of results to random-effects specification.
issues.quote: "Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model."

issues.description: The random-effects specification includes a random intercept of message, but each row appears to be a single message, making a random intercept for message unidentified or meaningless unless there are repeated observations per message. This raises concern that the model structure is conceptually or computationally misdescribed.
issues.quote: "a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message"

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide the exact model formulas, coding scheme for episode type contrasts, whether day was centered/scaled, whether overdispersion was checked, how zero-word or zero-category messages were handled, or how ratios were modeled. These omissions hinder replication and evaluation of model appropriateness.
issues.quote: "A series of mixed-effects models were performed..."

issues.description: Text messages are nested not only within participants and episodes but also within dyads/conversations/days. The manuscript does not report whether messages were grouped by recipient, conversation thread, or date, nor whether autocorrelation or clustering within days was addressed. This missing information prevents assessment of independence assumptions.
issues.quote: "Using mixed models allowed us to account for variability among participants, episodes, and messages"

issues.description: The paper says multiple follow-up questions were asked to minimize misclassification, but it does not report the exact criteria used to classify episodes into attempt, ideation, depressed, or positive/typical mood categories, nor whether independent raters reviewed classifications. This is crucial because episode type is the main predictor.
issues.quote: "Participants answered additional questions about each reported episode as a way to minimize the risk of misclassification"

issues.subcategory: unclear participant source and sampling frame
issues.description: The recruitment description mixes "Charlottesville community" with "participant pool participants" and semester pretests, suggesting a substantial student sample, but the exact sampling frame and proportions from student pool vs community are not reported. This obscures selection mechanisms and external validity.
issues.quote: "A sample of 33 participants with at least one reported past suicide attempt were recruited from the Charlottesville community." ... "Participant pool participants were selected based on two surveys"

issues.subcategory: substantial loss from recruited participants to analyzable SMS sample
issues.description: Only 27 of 33 participants had any episode with SMS data, and only 134 of 293 identified episodes (46%) contained SMS data. This is substantial missingness at both participant and episode levels. The manuscript does not adequately assess whether missingness was differential by episode type, phone type, time since event, or participant characteristics, so selection bias is a major concern.
issues.quote: "Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants."

issues.subcategory: missing data not plausibly missing at random
issues.description: The paper treats variable availability of episode types and text records as a type of missing data that mixed models can handle, but missing SMS history is likely structurally related to device changes, operating system, backup habits, and recency/severity of episodes. Mixed models do not solve bias from non-random missingness of this kind.
issues.quote: "this dataset given the amount of ‘missing data’ (i.e., participants varied widely in terms of the number of episodes types they reported and for which they had text data)."

issues.description: Message retrieval success differed by device and encryption settings, especially for iPhone users. This can systematically bias which episodes or participants contribute data and may correlate with age, SES, recency of messages, or texting practices. No analysis of these biases is reported.
issues.quote: "a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data."

issues.description: The study excludes individuals with high or imminent current risk. While ethically understandable, this likely selects for a less severe survivor sample and may bias the linguistic markers observed away from the population of greatest clinical concern. The implications for interpretation are not fully addressed.
issues.quote: "Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at “high risk” or “imminent risk” for suicidal behavior ... were excluded from study participation"

issues.description: The sample is small, predominantly female, White, and college-aged, with most having some college education. Claims about real-time suicide risk assessment in general populations are therefore overbroad. Findings may not generalize to males, older adults, clinically severe populations, nonstudents, or more diverse groups.
issues.quote: "Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged."

issues.subcategory: nonlethal/survivor sample generalized to suicide risk broadly
issues.description: The study necessarily uses nonfatal, mostly non-injurious, self-reported events and then discusses identifying suicide risk more broadly. Markers in this survivor sample may not generalize to medically serious attempts or suicide deaths.
issues.quote: "29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused ... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm"

issues.description: The study analyzes SMS messages only, yet extrapolates to private electronic communication and digital phenotyping more generally. Messaging behavior varies widely across platforms and populations, especially among younger users who may rely on apps other than SMS. Thus, conclusions should be limited to the observed channel.
issues.quote: "This study ... collected and analyze private text messaging data for suicide" ... "private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk."

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers to text-message language features as "digital biomarkers." Biomarker terminology usually implies a validated biological or objective indicator with known measurement properties; applying it to exploratory linguistic proxies is conceptually overstated and potentially misleading.
issues.quote: "possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors"

issues.subcategory: unsupported inference from social support theory to message counts
issues.description: The paper cites interpersonal theory and between-subjects perceived social support findings to justify hypotheses about incoming/outgoing SMS ratios. This is a large theoretical leap because perceived burdensomeness and belongingness are subjective states not directly indexed by message volume, making the prediction weakly grounded.
issues.quote: "In theory, social engagement should combat such feelings and increase feelings of connectedness... In the current study, we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement ... by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages."

issues.subcategory: real-time claim inconsistent with retrospective data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly emphasizes "real time" identification, but all episode labeling is retrospective and no real-time monitoring or prediction was conducted. This framing is internally inconsistent with the actual design and may overstate translational relevance.
issues.quote: "Can Text Messages Identify Suicide Risk in Real Time?" ... "retrospectively identified past attempts and periods of lower risk"

issues.subcategory: missing exact numbers by episode type with SMS data
issues.description: The manuscript reports 134 episodes with SMS data and says participants had on average 1.5 episodes for each type, but it does not provide the exact number of analyzable attempt, ideation, depressed, and positive/typical episodes. Without this, readers cannot judge balance, power for specific contrasts, or whether some episode types were sparsely represented.
issues.quote: "Among these 27 participants, all had data from at least one reported suicide attempt. Participants reported and had SMS data for on average approximately 1.5 episodes for each episode type."

issues.subcategory: no information on missing message content preprocessing
issues.description: The cleaning and de-identification procedures are described generally, but there is no detail on handling emojis, non-English texts, group messages, duplicates, media-only messages, misspellings, URLs, timestamps, or whether incoming and outgoing messages were both subjected to identical preprocessing. These decisions can materially affect LIWC scores.
issues.quote: "participants’ SMS data files were individually cleaned using Python to standardize the encoding of messages and naming of variables across all participants."
